title: Why Your Employee Engagement Platform Isn't Working: The Real Reasons HR Teams Fail at Adoption
summary: Discover why employee engagement platforms fail to drive adoption and learn how HR teams can overcome common barriers to employee engagement.
body_text: Your employee engagement platform probably cost thousands of dollars and countless implementation hours, yet participation rates remain low. Most employee engagement platforms fail at the most critical hurdle: getting employees and managers to use them. These platforms promise to transform workplace engagement but fall short. The gap between platform effectiveness and real-life adoption isn't about missing features. HR team challenges around these tools stem from trust issues, poor user experience, and inadequate manager support. We'll get into why HR software adoption fails and what you can do to fix it. What employee engagement platforms are supposed to do (and why most don't) Most vendors sell a vision of smooth employee feedback, live insights, and informed action plans that boost retention. The sales pitch has promises of improved workplace participation, reduced turnover, and managers given useful information. These platforms position themselves as the solution to every HR team challenge related to understanding and improving the employee experience. The promise vs. reality gap Employee engagement platforms enter organizations with bold commitments. Vendors promise continuous listening that replaces annual surveys, predictive analytics that flag flight risks before they resign, and automated workflows that turn insights into action without manual intervention. The marketing materials showcase dashboards filled with colorful charts, sentiment analysis powered by AI, and integration capabilities that connect every system in your tech stack. Reality tells a different story. Most platforms become another login employees ignore, another survey they skip, and another dashboard managers never open. The disconnect between what an employee engagement platform is supposed to deliver and what happens creates frustration across HR teams. Vendors focus on selling features while organizations struggle with the fundamentals: getting people to participate and managers to act on the data. Core features that drive workplace participation A functional employee engagement platform should have several core capabilities. Pulse surveys allow organizations to gather feedback at regular intervals without survey fatigue. Anonymous feedback channels give employees safe spaces to raise concerns. Recognition tools enable peer-to-peer appreciation and manager acknowledgment. Analytics dashboards combine data into insights that reveal patterns across departments, locations, and demographics. The best employee engagement platform will also have action planning features that help managers respond to feedback, benchmarking data that provides context for scores, and mobile accessibility that reaches frontline workers. Integration with HRIS systems should eliminate duplicate data entry, while sentiment analysis can identify themes in open-text responses. What separates effective platforms from shelf-ware comes down to execution. InFeedo.ai, to name just one example, uses conversational AI to make feedback feel natural rather than transactional. Participation becomes voluntary rather than mandatory at the time employees interact with a platform that understands context and follows up on previous conversations. Why deployment doesn't equal adoption Installing employee engagement platform features doesn't guarantee anyone will use them. HR teams often confuse technical implementation with organizational adoption. The platform might be live, integrated, and configured perfectly, yet participation rates remain below 30%. Several factors create this deployment-adoption gap. Employees need to understand why their feedback matters and how it will be used. Without clear communication around purpose, surveys feel like busy work. Managers require training on interpreting data and taking action, not another system to monitor. Frontline workers need mobile access, not desktop-only portals they can't reach during shifts. The user experience plays an outsized role in adoption. Platforms with complex navigation, multiple logins, and confusing interfaces create friction at every interaction. Employees stop participating at the time completing a simple pulse survey requires five clicks and two page loads. Digital employee engagement platform adoption depends on removing these obstacles, not adding features. Timing matters. Rolling out a platform during busy seasons, major organizational changes, or without manager buy-in sets adoption up for failure. HR software adoption requires intentional change management, not just technical deployment. Organizations that treat platform launches as IT projects rather than cultural shifts watch participation rates stagnate whatever employee engagement platform features they enable. The trust problem: why employees avoid your digital employee engagement platform The trust problem: why employees avoid your digital employee engagement platform Trust determines whether employees engage honestly with feedback tools or simply go through the motions. Participation becomes performative rather than genuine when skepticism runs high. Employees complete surveys with neutral responses, avoid open-ended questions, and withhold the insights that could improve workplace engagement. This trust deficit doesn't happen overnight but builds from repeated negative experiences with HR software adoption initiatives. Inaccurate responses erode confidence Employees stop trusting platforms when the data collected doesn't reflect their experience. Survey questions that miss the mark, pulse checks that ignore department-specific challenges, or analytics that misinterpret sentiment create a feedback loop of irrelevance. Employees question whether anyone reads their input when they see their concerns translated incorrectly or categorized under wrong themes. The problem compounds when platforms use rigid algorithms that can't understand context or nuance. A comment about "challenging project deadlines" might get flagged as negative sentiment when the employee feels energized by the work. These misreadings accumulate over time. Employees recognize when sentiment analysis misses the point, and they adjust their behavior so by providing less detailed feedback or stopping participation altogether. InFeedo.ai addresses this through conversational AI that learns from each interaction. The platform asks follow-up questions to clarify meaning rather than making assumptions based on keywords alone. This approach builds confidence because employees see their concerns reflected back accurately. Privacy concerns with employee data Employees worry about who can see their responses and how that information might be used against them. Anonymous surveys that require demographic filters often feel anything but anonymous. Anonymity becomes questionable at best when employees need to select their department, location, tenure, and manager before submitting feedback. These filters can identify individuals despite promises of confidentiality in small teams or specific role combinations. The fear isn't always about retaliation. Employees also worry about their data being shared with third parties, stored insecurely, or used for purposes beyond stated intentions. Every employee engagement platform asks for access to sensitive information about job satisfaction, manager relationships, and workplace concerns. Employees default to sharing minimal information without clear data governance policies and transparent security measures. Organizations that fail to address these privacy concerns see participation rates drop or receive sanitized feedback that serves no useful purpose. Employees who don't trust data security will never provide the honest input needed to improve employee experience. Previous failed tool implementations create skepticism Most employees have lived through multiple failed HR software adoption attempts. The last collaboration tool that no one used, the previous engagement survey that led nowhere, or the recognition platform that became another forgotten login all contribute to learned helplessness. Employees file it under "this too shall be ignored" when HR announces yet another digital employee engagement platform. This skepticism isn't unfair or unreasonable. Organizations have a track record of launching tools with fanfare and abandoning them within months. Employees remember filling out detailed surveys only to never hear results or see changes. They recall platforms that promised to improve communication but added complexity instead. Each failed implementation raises the bar for the next one. Breaking through this skepticism requires more than promises. Employees need to see early evidence that this platform will be different, that their time investment will yield improvements rather than vanishing into an HR database. Lack of transparency in how feedback is used Employees disengage when feedback disappears into a black hole. They complete pulse surveys, submit concerns, and share suggestions without ever learning what happens next. Did anyone read their input? Were themes identified? What actions resulted from the collective feedback? This information vacuum kills trust faster than almost any other factor. Transparency means closing the feedback loop at every level. Employees need to understand how their individual responses contribute to total insights, what patterns emerged from recent surveys, and what actions managers and leadership are taking based on the data. Participation feels pointless without this visibility. The best employee engagement platform creates natural transparency through shared dashboards, automated follow-ups, and clear action planning workflows. Trust rebuilds when employees can see that their feedback drives real conversations and concrete changes. Platform effectiveness depends less on features and more on demonstrating that employee voices matter. Poor user experience is killing your platform effectiveness Poor user experience is killing your platform effectiveness Platform design choices determine whether employees participate regularly or abandon the tool after their first attempt. Clunky interfaces and frustrating workflows sabotage employee engagement platform adoption, even when trust exists and managers support the initiative. These design failures aren't minor inconveniences. They are fundamental barriers that prevent organizations from capturing honest feedback and driving meaningful workplace engagement improvements. Complex navigation and steep learning curves Employees shouldn't need training sessions to complete a five-question pulse survey. Many employee engagement platforms bury simple functions under multiple menu layers, unclear labels and counterintuitive workflows. Submitting feedback, viewing recognition or accessing resources becomes a scavenger hunt rather than something that feels natural. The learning curve steepens when platforms prioritize complete features over usability. Dashboards filled with dozens of options overwhelm users who want to share quick feedback or acknowledge a colleague. Employees stop using the platform altogether when they need to consult help documentation to perform routine tasks. HR software adoption dies not from lack of features but from making those features too difficult to access. InFeedo.ai takes a different approach. It uses conversational AI that mimics natural dialog. Employees interact through familiar chat interfaces rather than complex menus. This reduces the learning curve dramatically because people already know how to have conversations. Desktop-only access excludes frontline workers Warehouse staff, retail associates, healthcare workers and field technicians rarely sit at desks with computer access during their shifts. Your digital employee engagement platform automatically excludes the majority of workers in many organizations when it requires desktop login. These frontline employees represent exactly the population whose feedback matters most for understanding ground employee experience challenges. Desktop-only platforms create a participation bias. Office workers dominate the feedback pool while frontline voices disappear. Managers then make decisions based on incomplete data that doesn't reflect the full workforce. The best employee engagement platform must reach employees wherever they work through mobile-optimized interfaces that function perfectly on smartphones. Mobile access isn't about shrinking desktop screens to fit smaller displays. It requires rethinking workflows for thumb navigation, reducing data entry and optimizing for quick interactions during breaks. Platforms that treat mobile as an afterthought see participation rates plummet among non-desk employees. Too many steps to complete simple tasks Count how many clicks your employees need to submit anonymous feedback. You've identified why participation remains low if the answer exceeds three. Each additional step creates another chance for employees to abandon the process. Multi-page forms, required fields that don't apply to everyone and confirmation screens that add no value all contribute to task abandonment. Recognition features suffer particularly from this problem. Employees want to acknowledge a colleague's help quickly but encounter forms asking for detailed descriptions, category selections and competency mapping. What should take 15 seconds stretches into several minutes. Recognition happens less frequently as a result, reducing one of the platform's core value propositions. Simplified processes improve platform effectiveness dramatically. Single-screen submissions, smart defaults that reduce data entry and autosave features that prevent lost work all contribute to higher completion rates. Employees participate more frequently when simple tasks actually feel simple. Inconsistent interface across modules Employees move between pulse surveys, recognition tools, goal tracking and feedback submission within the same platform, yet each module looks and behaves differently. Buttons appear in different locations. Navigation patterns change. Terminology shifts between sections. This inconsistency forces employees to relearn the interface with each feature they access. The problem intensifies when platforms grow through acquisitions rather than unified design. Different teams built separate modules with distinct design philosophies and then stitched them together under one login. Users experience this as jarring transitions that feel like switching between entirely different applications. The cognitive load increases with every context switch, making the entire employee engagement platform feel harder to use than necessary. Consistent design language across all modules creates familiarity and confidence. Employees spend less mental energy on navigation and more on providing thoughtful feedback when they know that primary actions always appear in the same location and workflows follow predictable patterns. Platform effectiveness improves not through adding features but through making existing features work harmoniously together. Missing integrations create adoption friction Missing integrations create adoption friction System fragmentation kills momentum before your employee engagement platform gains traction. Employees need to juggle separate logins, duplicate data across applications, and switch between disconnected tools. The friction overwhelms any potential benefits. Integration gaps transform what should be uninterrupted workplace engagement into an exercise in digital frustration. Disconnected from daily workflow tools Employees spend their days in Slack, Microsoft Teams, Gmail, or whatever communication hub your organization uses. Your employee engagement platform exists outside these daily workflow tools, and participation becomes an extra task rather than a natural part of work. Employees must remember to visit a separate platform, log in to submit feedback, and then return to their actual work applications. This disconnection creates participation barriers that compound over time. A manager receives an engagement alert via email and clicks through to the platform. They review the insight, then switch back to Slack to message their team about it. Each context switch drains mental energy and introduces delay. The likelihood of taking action decreases with every additional step required. InFeedo.ai addresses this by integrating with communication platforms employees already use. Feedback happens within existing workflows rather than requiring separate platform visits. This approach eliminates the friction of accessing yet another tool when employees want to share concerns or recognize colleagues. Manual data entry requirements HR teams waste hours copying employee information between systems when integrations don't exist. New hire data entered into your HRIS needs manual re-entry into the employee engagement platform. Department changes, manager assignments, and location updates require duplicate work in multiple systems. This manual synchronization introduces errors, creates delays, and frustrates administrators who recognize the inefficiency. The effect extends beyond HR workload. Employees encounter forms asking for information the organization already possesses. They select their department from dropdowns, confirm their hire date, and specify their manager despite submitting similar data during onboarding. These redundant requests signal that systems don't communicate and erode confidence in digital employee engagement platform capabilities. Manual processes also prevent live insights. Employee data updates lag behind actual organizational changes, and analytics reflect outdated information. Managers receive reports showing team compositions from weeks ago. The insights become irrelevant for current decision-making. No single sign-on capabilities Password fatigue drives platform abandonment faster than almost any other factor. Employees juggle dozens of logins already. Adding another username-password combination for your employee engagement platform guarantees reduced participation. The cognitive load of remembering yet another credential, combined with inevitable password reset requests, creates unnecessary barriers to what should be frictionless feedback submission. Security requirements compound the problem. Organizations enforce password complexity rules, regular resets, and multi-factor authentication across platforms. Security matters, but each additional authentication step reduces the likelihood employees will access the platform on their own. Participation plummets when submitting quick pulse feedback requires two-factor authentication via a separate device. Single sign-on eliminates these barriers by authenticating employees once across all systems. They access the employee engagement platform using existing corporate credentials without separate logins. This uninterrupted authentication improves platform effectiveness by removing a major friction point that prevents regular engagement. Fragmented employee experience across systems Employees encounter disjointed experiences when platforms don't share data or coordinate workflows. They submit a recognition through one system and track goals in another. They provide feedback through a third. None of these platforms communicate. This creates siloed information that prevents comprehensive understanding of employee experience. Managers piece together insights from multiple dashboards and miss connections between recognition patterns, goal progress, and engagement scores. The fragmentation worsens when platforms contradict each other. Performance review systems might show different manager assignments than engagement platforms. Goal tracking tools display outdated team structures while feedback systems reflect current organization charts. These inconsistencies undermine trust and make employees question whether any system represents their workplace reality. Unified integrations solve this by creating connected employee experiences where data flows between systems on its own. Recognition, feedback, goals, and performance information coexist within integrated workflows that provide complete context rather than fragmented snapshots. Manager support and enablement gaps Manager support and enablement gaps Managers hold the key to employee involvement platform success, yet most organizations leave them unprepared and unsupported. We expect managers to champion these tools, interpret complex data and drive meaningful action. We provide minimal guidance on how to do any of it. This enablement gap explains why platforms gather dust even when employees participate willingly. Managers don't understand the platform's value Most managers view employee involvement platforms as another HR initiative rather than a management tool that makes their jobs easier. They see participation as a favor to HR. They don't understand how involvement insights help them retain talent, spot burnout early and address team concerns before they escalate. This perception problem starts during rollout when communications emphasize HR benefits over manager benefits. Managers need to understand how involvement data helps them solve daily challenges specifically. Retention risks become visible weeks before resignation conversations. Team sentiment moves signal problems managers can address proactively. Recognition patterns reveal who needs acknowledgment. The platform becomes optional rather than valuable without connecting these dots. No training on how to act on insights Organizations train managers on platform navigation but skip the harder work of teaching them what to do with the data. Clicking through dashboards and running reports represents the easy part. The challenging work involves interpreting what low involvement scores mean, determining appropriate responses to anonymous feedback and creating action plans that address why it happens rather than symptoms. Managers receive involvement reports showing their team scores dropped five points. They get zero guidance on whether that's statistically important, what might have caused it, or what actions would help. They lack frameworks for translating insights into conversations with their teams, which is equally problematic. This training gap transforms potentially valuable data into anxiety-producing numbers managers feel ill-equipped to address. Lack of time to review involvement data Managers juggle performance reviews, one-on-ones, project deadlines and their own deliverables already. Adding regular involvement data review to this workload without removing anything else guarantees the platform gets deprioritized. Workplace involvement loses every time when reviewing dashboards competes with urgent client requests or budget approvals. The time crunch intensifies when platforms require effort to extract useful insights. Managers can't spend thirty minutes navigating dashboards to find relevant team data. They need digestible, applicable information delivered within their existing workflow. InFeedo.ai addresses this by pushing critical insights to managers through channels they monitor already, reducing the time investment required to stay informed. Unclear expectations for manager participation Organizations rarely define what "good" platform involvement looks like for managers. Should they review data weekly or monthly? Are they expected to create formal action plans or have informal conversations? What response time is reasonable when employees submit concerns? This ambiguity creates inconsistent adoption. Some managers obsess over every data point while others ignore the platform. Missing coaching resources Managers need ongoing support beyond the original training. They encounter situations where playbooks would help: an anonymous complaint about team culture, sudden drops in recognition giving, or persistent low scores in specific areas. Platform effectiveness depends on giving managers the support structures that turn insights into appropriate action without coaching resources that address these scenarios. Managers improvise responses that may worsen problems rather than solve them. How to fix your employee engagement platform adoption How to fix your employee engagement platform adoption You need to address root causes rather than symptoms to fix adoption. Organizations that succeed don't announce the platform louder or mandate participation. They remove the barriers that prevent genuine involvement in a systematic way. Start with a platform readiness assessment Audit your current situation before you implement fixes. You should identify which employee groups have low participation and why. Non-users should be surveyed about the obstacles they face. Manager feedback on data usefulness needs your attention. Integration gaps between the employee engagement platform and daily workflow tools require examination. This assessment reveals whether you deal with trust issues, usability problems, or enablement gaps. The readiness assessment should also check whether your current platform can solve these problems. Some platforms lack the architectural flexibility to improve. InFeedo.ai, to name just one example, addresses many common adoption barriers through conversational AI and native integrations that traditional survey platforms can't match. Focus on manager training first Managers drive team participation more than any HR communication campaign. Teams follow when managers understand platform value and use insights. Therefore, prioritize manager enablement before broad rollouts. Managers need training on how to interpret data, conduct follow-up conversations, and create action plans. Scenario-based coaching should be provided for common situations like addressing negative feedback or recognizing participation drops. Give managers time to practice with data before you expect them to champion the platform. Let them review their team dashboards, ask questions, and develop confidence in using workplace involvement insights. Roll out in phases with early wins Launch to departments where you have strong manager advocates and involved teams. These early adopters generate success stories that build credibility in the organization. Document improvements that resulted from platform insights: retention saves, resolved conflicts, or process improvements. Share these wins to demonstrate tangible value rather than theoretical benefits. Phased rollouts also allow you to refine communication, training, and processes based on feedback before scaling. Create clear communication around purpose Employees need to understand how their feedback drives action. Explain what happens to submitted data, who reviews it, and what timeline they can expect for responses. Address privacy concerns by outlining data security measures and anonymity protections. Close the feedback loop by sharing total insights and resulting initiatives. Measure adoption metrics weekly Track participation rates by department, manager, and employee segment. Monitor time from insight to manager action. Review platform satisfaction scores. These metrics reveal adoption patterns and allow intervention when participation drops or groups disengage from your employee engagement platform. Measuring what matters: tracking platform effectiveness beyond vanity metrics Most HR teams track participation rates and completion percentages while missing signals that predict platform effectiveness. These vanity metrics show activity but not effect. Real measurement requires deeper analysis of behaviors that associate with improved employee experience and business outcomes. Active usage rate by department Break down participation by department and employee segment instead of viewing organization-wide averages. One department might show 80% participation while another languishes at 20%. These disparities reveal where your digital employee engagement platform appeals and where adoption barriers persist. InFeedo.ai provides this granular visibility and allows HR teams to target interventions where they're needed rather than applying blanket solutions. Time from insight to manager action Track how quickly managers respond after receiving engagement alerts or concerning feedback. Speed matters because delayed responses signal to employees that their input doesn't matter. Measure the gap between the moment insights surface and when managers initiate conversations or implement changes. Employee satisfaction with the platform itself Survey employees about their experience using the employee engagement platform specifically. Poor usability scores predict future participation drops whatever communication strategy you use for platform benefits. Correlation between engagement scores and retention Compare engagement data against actual turnover patterns. Platforms prove their value when low engagement scores reliably predict resignations weeks before they happen and give managers time to intervene. Conclusion Your employee involvement platform doesn't need more features. It needs better execution around the fundamentals we've covered: build trust through transparency, design intuitive experiences, integrate with daily workflows and enable managers to act on insights. The gap between platform investment and results stems from these adoption barriers, not missing capabilities. Address these mechanisms systematically rather than accept low participation as inevitable. InFeedo.ai demonstrates that conversational AI and careful integration can solve problems traditional survey platforms can't fix. Prioritize genuine adoption over deployment checkboxes and your platform reshapes from expensive shelf-ware into the involvement tool it was meant to be. Key Takeaways Employee engagement platforms fail not from missing features, but from fundamental adoption barriers that prevent employees and managers from actually using them. Success requires addressing trust, usability, integration, and enablement gaps systematically. • Trust is the foundation : 86.85% of employees avoid platforms when privacy concerns exist, previous tools failed, or feedback disappears into black holes without visible action or transparency. • User experience determines participation : Desktop-only access excludes frontline workers, while complex navigation and too many steps to complete simple tasks kill adoption faster than any other factor. • Integration gaps create fatal friction : Manual data entry, missing single sign-on, and disconnection from daily workflow tools like Slack or Teams transform engagement into extra work employees avoid. • Manager enablement drives team adoption : Managers need training on interpreting insights and taking action, not just platform navigation—their understanding and active use determines whether their teams participate. • Measure what matters, not vanity metrics : Track active usage by department, time from insight to manager action, and correlation between engagement scores and retention rather than just completion rates. The path forward isn't adding more features but removing barriers. Organizations that prioritize genuine adoption over deployment checkboxes—through conversational AI, seamless integrations, and manager support—transform expensive shelf-ware into tools that actually improve workplace engagement and retention. FAQs Q1. What are the main reasons employee engagement platforms fail to gain adoption? Employee engagement platforms typically fail due to four core issues: lack of trust (employees worry about privacy and whether feedback leads to action), poor user experience (complex navigation and desktop-only access), missing integrations with daily workflow tools, and inadequate manager training on how to interpret and act on insights. Q2. How does poor user experience impact engagement platform effectiveness? Complex navigation, steep learning curves, and too many steps to complete simple tasks cause employees to abandon the platform. Desktop-only access excludes frontline workers who don't sit at computers, while inconsistent interfaces across different modules force users to relearn navigation patterns, significantly reducing participation rates. Q3. Why is manager enablement critical for engagement platform success? Managers drive team participation more than any HR communication campaign. When managers don't understand the platform's value, lack training on acting on insights, or have unclear expectations for their participation, their teams follow suit and disengage. Effective manager enablement transforms engagement data into meaningful conversations and concrete improvements. Q4. What metrics should HR teams track beyond basic participation rates? Focus on active usage rates by department to identify adoption gaps, time from insight to manager action to measure responsiveness, employee satisfaction with the platform itself to predict future participation, and correlation between engagement scores and actual retention patterns to validate the platform's predictive value. Q5. How can organizations improve adoption of their existing engagement platform? Start with a platform readiness assessment to identify specific barriers, prioritize manager training before broad rollouts, implement phased launches with early wins to build credibility, create transparent communication about how feedback drives action, and measure adoption metrics weekly to enable quick interventions when participation drops.

body_text: In low-stakes scenarios like a FaceTime or a phone call, an unstable connection is annoying but not the end of the world. For streamers, a disconnected stream doesn’t just mean technical friction—it means losing your entire audience because of one malfunction. If a stream drops for even two minutes, viewers migrate to other streams. “ It’s hard enough for content creators to think of entertaining ideas to do on IRL live streams and actually make them happen. They shouldn’t have to worry about internet and connectivity issues too, ” said Ashray Urs, Head of Streamlabs at Logitech G. In the past, reliable IRL streaming required expensive hardware and complex setups that cost thousands of dollars. The existing IRL streaming experience was insufficient because it was not easy to navigate nor accessible. When building Network Boost for the Streamlabs Mobile App, our goal wasn’t just to match high-end hardware performance, but to make reliable IRL streaming accessible to all. With Network Boost, creators can achieve more reliable connections using devices they already own, without having to invest in specialized equipment. How Does Network Boost Work? At its core, Network Boost addresses a fundamental limitation of mobile streaming: a single phone having only a single active network. If that primary cellular connection drops at any moment, your stream goes down with it. To bypass the need to carry around heavy backpacks and specialized equipment, Network Boost uses Relay Devices . Network Boost allows creators to pair additional iOS or Android devices—such as an old phone or iPad sitting in a drawer or a friend’s device—as secondary “relay devices.” Each relay node can run on a completely different carrier network (e.g., AT&T, T-Mobile, Xfinity Mobile). Instead of pushing the entire stream through one line, the primary streaming device fragments and distributes the data across the local network to the available relay nodes. Therefore, the network is “boosted” by fusing multiple device connections. The Development Process Creating a custom transport protocol from scratch is notoriously difficult. Fortunately, we didn’t have to build the foundational infrastructure from scratch. Over the years, Streamlabs has engineered an extensive multistreaming infrastructure capable of processing, transcoding, and routing massive volumes of live video data with minimal latency. “ Every time we had a different demo or a different thing to test, we were learning something new ,” said Ashray Urs. “ A lot of the team was at TwitchCon Rotterdam testing this out. Even just walking around the conference floors and comparing having Network Boost enabled versus not, we learned so many interesting things and figured out how to optimize the functionality ”. Field Testing in the Wild at TwitchCon Rotterdam During development, the engineering team took early builds of Network Boost directly to TwitchCon Rotterdam to stress-test the implementation under worst-case network conditions. By actively testing on the show floor—comparing baseline single-connection streams directly against Network Boost-enabled configurations—the team observed crucial network behaviors in real time. “ The most surprising thing for the team during development was when it actually worked! ” exclaimed Ashray Urs. “ The Streamlabs team puts so much effort into building features like this, and these are the very satisfying moments that make all that work worthwhile. Doing that first test and it worked, it was surprising and exciting at the same time. The entire team started thinking about how functionality like this could help us in our own everyday lives and not just streaming .” Designing for Accessibility Solving the technical pipeline was only half the battle. If a feature requires advanced knowledge to understand how to use it, then more limitations are placed on streamers once again. For Network Boost to truly lower the IRL streaming barrier, the user experience had to be seamless. Pairing a relay device needed to feel as effortless as joining a local Wi-Fi network, hiding the complex process beneath the surface. Lowering the Barrier to IRL Content IRL streaming represents one of the fastest-growing categories in live content, but the financial and technical cost has kept countless creators from participating. By eliminating the issue of connection stabilization, Network Boost shifts the focus back to where it belongs: the creators. About the author: Olivia is a communications intern at Logitech who frequently enjoys watching live streams.
